issues.legal_issue: A subsequent purchaser is not exempt from specific performance when the purchaser fails to establish that the purchase was made in good faith without notice of the earlier contract.
material_facts: The owner entered into an agreement to sell the property to the plaintiff and later transferred the property to the appellants.
The appellants claimed to be purchasers for value without notice of the earlier agreement.
The plaintiff and the appellants conducted similar businesses in adjoining premises and lived in the same locality.
The trial court and High Court found, on the evidence and surrounding circumstances, that the appellants had notice of the earlier agreement and were not bona fide purchasers.
issues.conclusion: The appellants were not protected as bona fide purchasers for value without notice, so the decree for specific performance could be enforced against them.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 19(b) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, a subsequent transferee is excepted from enforcement of a contract only if the transferee paid value in good faith and without notice of the original contract; the subsequent purchaser bears the burden of proving good faith. Good faith requires due care and attention under Section 52 of the Penal Code, while the General Clauses Act emphasizes honesty. The court assessed notice and good faith from the evidence and circumstances, consistent with the approach in Dr. Govinddas v. Shrimati Shantibai and the authorities discussed there.

rule.if: specific_performance_case and prior_contract and later_property_transfer and purchaser_claims_good_faith and (purchaser_had_actual_notice or purchaser_failed_to_make_required_inquiry)

predicates.specific_performance_case: A claimant seeks specific performance of an agreement to sell property against a later purchaser.
predicates.prior_contract: The property owner made an agreement to sell the property to the claimant before transferring it to the later purchaser.
predicates.later_property_transfer: The owner transferred the property to the later purchaser after making the earlier agreement.
predicates.purchaser_claims_good_faith: The later purchaser asserts that the purchase was made in good faith without notice of the earlier agreement.
predicates.purchaser_had_actual_notice: The later purchaser knew of the earlier agreement when acquiring the property.
predicates.purchaser_failed_to_make_required_inquir: The later purchaser failed to make an inquiry that a prudent purchaser in the circumstances should have made.
predicates.subsequent_purchaser_not_protected_from_: The later purchaser does not qualify for the protection that would prevent enforcement of the earlier agreement against the purchaser.

issues.definition: When a later purchaser claims good faith but had actual notice or failed to make a required inquiry, the purchaser is not protected from specific performance of the earlier agreement.

issues.legal_issue: A purchaser of property in another person's actual possession must inquire into the nature of that possession and any further interest, even if the purchaser knows the person occupies the property as a tenant.
material_facts: The plaintiff had occupied the property as a tenant for many years and used it as a business godown.
The appellants knew that the plaintiff was in possession as a tenant when they purchased the property.
The property adjoined the plaintiff's business premises, and the appellants operated a similar business nearby.
The appellants did not inquire whether the plaintiff had any further interest in the property, although an earlier sale agreement existed in the plaintiff's favour.
issues.conclusion: The appellants were required to inquire into the plaintiff's further interest at the time of purchase; their failure to do so meant they had constructive notice of that interest and were not purchasers without notice.
issues.legal_principle: Section 3 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 defines notice to include knowledge imputed where a person willfully abstains from an inquiry that ought to have been made or is grossly negligent. Explanation II to Section 3 deems a person acquiring immovable property to have notice of the title, if any, of the person in actual possession. A purchaser must inquire into the possessor's nature of possession and title as they stand at the time of purchase, including interests beyond a known tenancy. The court relied on Daniels v. Davision, Mummidi Reddi Papannagari Yella Reddy v. Salla Subbi Reddy, Veeramalai Vanniar v. Thadikara Vanniar, and Dr. Govinddas v. Shrimati Shantibai.

rule.if: specific_performance_case and prior_contract and later_property_transfer and purchaser_knew_of_possession and possessor_was_tenant and purchaser_did_not_inquire_into_further_interest

predicates.specific_performance_case: A claimant seeks specific performance of an agreement to sell property against a later purchaser.
predicates.prior_contract: The property owner made an agreement to sell the property to the claimant before transferring it to the later purchaser.
predicates.later_property_transfer: The owner transferred the property to the later purchaser after making the earlier agreement.
predicates.purchaser_knew_of_possession: The later purchaser knew that another person was in actual possession of the property when the purchase was made.
predicates.possessor_was_tenant: The person in possession occupied the property as a tenant.
predicates.purchaser_did_not_inquire_into_further_i: The later purchaser did not ask whether the person in possession had any interest in the property beyond the known tenancy.
predicates.purchaser_has_constructive_notice_of_pos: The later purchaser is treated as having notice of the further interest held by the person in possession.

issues.definition: When a later purchaser knows that a tenant is in actual possession but does not inquire into any further interest, the purchaser is treated as having notice of that interest.
